seo.title: Karmic tail 9 6 6 compatibility: the Hermit and the Lovers twice
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 6 6 compatibility in the destiny matrix: the Hermit at the entry, the Lovers in the middle and the main task. Why the couple hides its love.

title: Karmic tail 9-6-6 in compatibility: love under the Hermit's cloak
short: The karmic tail 9-6-6 in destiny matrix compatibility is the Hermit at the entry and the Lovers twice in a row, in the middle and in the main task. The couple comes together through quiet, depth and a language of its own, and it has one thing to learn: not to hide its love from each other as carefully as it hides it from the world.

sections.h2: Why no single person has the tail 9-6-6
paragraphs: Every point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The middle of the couple is not derived from its outer numbers; it is added up from the partners' own middles. That makes 9-6-6 a tail born only between two people. It occurs in roughly one couple in 97 (1.026%) and ranks 36th of the 97 couple tails.

The site's engine finds nine combinations of personal tails that produce 9-6-6. The most common are 3-7-22 + 6-17-11 (25% of such couples), 18-3-12 + 9-3-21 (22%) and 21-4-10 + 6-20-14 (17%). The couple's middle is assembled from other people's middles: the Chariot and the Star (7 + 17 = 24 → 6), two Empresses (3 + 3), the Emperor and Judgement (4 + 20 = 24 → 6).
Three clues are hidden in these nine combinations.

**First: neither partner has the Lovers as a main task.** The partners' personal main tasks in these combinations are 22 and 11, 12 and 21, 10 and 14, 12 and 12, 13 and 11, 19 and 14, 15 and 9, 16 and 8. A six never appears. The couple's task exists only once the two are side by side.

**Second: one partner's love becomes the couple's quiet.** In about three couples out of five (61% across the combinations) one partner enters their own personal tail through the Lovers: 6-17-11, 6-20-14, 6-14-8. Yet the couple enters through the Hermit: 6 + 3 = 9, or 6 + 21 = 27 → 9. Our reading: someone who starts with love when alone starts with quiet next to this partner. The Lovers come back to the couple later, as the road and as the test.

**Third: the Hermit is not there to be defeated.** In the couple's values, such unions have the Hermit in 70.2% of cases and the Moon in 29.8%. For seven couples out of ten, the card of quiet is not only the entry but what the union exists for. So the task is not to stop being hermits.

In the atmosphere inside the couple, 56.7% of such unions have the World, 38.7% the Hanged Man and 4.6% the Empress. No date of birth puts the World in the centre of a personal chart: this card reaches the centre only for two. Waite's divinatory list for the World reads "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place". For a couple this is no forecast of a move; it is the air between two people, the feeling that together they have a whole world.

paragraphs.h3: Example: two people born on the same day

paragraphs: The example uses the dates 05.12.1975 and 05.12.1975, a couple who share a birthday. Each has the personal tail 18-3-12, the Lovers (6) in the centre of the chart and the Hermit (9) in the spiritual purpose.

In the couple the same two cards come out into the tail and become a task. What each of them keeps inside, the two of them will have to do.

sections.h2: The room in Wimpole Street: entering through the Hermit
paragraphs: On 10 January 1845, Robert Browning, aged thirty-two, writes a letter to Elizabeth Barrett. She is thirty-eight, one of the best-known poets in England, and for years she has hardly left her room at 50 Wimpole Street. The letter opens: "I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett", and in the middle stands: "and I love you too."

He goes on to recall how he once nearly saw her: a mutual friend went up to announce him, but she was too unwell. "As if I had been close, so close, to some world's-wonder in chapel or crypt, only a screen to push and I might have entered… and the half-opened door shut." She answers the next day and takes up his word: had he entered the "crypt", he "might have caught cold". "Winters shut me up as they do dormouse's eyes; in the spring, we shall see."

In spring she writes: "You are Paracelsus, and I am a recluse." And explains: "I have lived only inwardly." Before his first visit she prepares him for disappointment: "There is nothing to see in me; nor to hear in me… If my poetry is worth anything to any eye, it is the flower of me… the rest of me is nothing but a root, fit for the ground and the dark." And at once she sets a condition: "You will not talk of having come afterwards I know."
The first meeting is on Tuesday, 20 May 1845. On the envelope of her letter Robert writes: "Tuesday, May 20, 1845, 3-4½ p.m." He marked every meeting this way, to the last.

This is the Hermit at the entry to the task. Point M is what the couple wants together, its common language. Two people with the tail 9-6-6 want not a noisy crowd but a conversation where the important things can be said. They take every step slowly and show love by deeds before words. Benebell Wen notes that the Hermit's lantern can be read as light for others, or as the sign of "someone who sees the world through his or her own light". Two people with this entry recognise each other by that kind of light.

But point M stands on the line of tasks, so here the wish turns into resistance. The very letter that invites him says "there is nothing to see in me" and asks him to keep the visit quiet. The Hermit lets people in only by appointment: "any day after two, or before six". In a couple today it looks like this: two people text each other until three in the morning and know more about each other than friends of ten years, yet when one asks "how are you?", each answers "fine".

sections.h2: The missing letter: the middle of the task
paragraphs: The correspondence survives almost entire, 573 letters. The poets' son published it in 1899 and described how it was kept: Robert held the letters in an inlaid box into which they exactly fitted, "letter beside letter, each in its consecutive order and numbered on the envelope by his own hand". One letter is missing from that box.

After the first meeting Robert wrote something she did not expect, most likely a declaration. Three days later she replies: "You have said some intemperate things… which you will not say over again, nor unsay, but forget at once, and for ever, having said at all; and which (so) will die out between you and me alone, like a misprint between you and the printer." And she adds that if one word of answer is attempted, "I will not see you again." Robert asked for the letter back and destroyed it. Half a year later she asks for it herself. He replies: "Could you think that that untoward letter lived one moment after it returned to me? I burned it and cried 'serve it right'!"

Here are the first Lovers of this tail. The middle of the task is where the word of love finally sounds, and at once the Hermit asks for it to be treated as a misprint. Wen writes that the Lovers are the beginnings of romance, and that the feeling of paradise on this card "may be evanescent if caution is not observed". In a 9-6-6 couple caution is built into the entry itself. It guards love and nearly smothers it. The couple passes the middle when it learns not to burn the first letter.

The second half of the middle is a choice. For Wen the Lovers are above all a card of choice, and this choice cannot be made halfway. Elizabeth's father disinherited each of his children who married without his permission, and he never gave permission to anyone. So the choice is made in secret.

Saturday, 12 September 1846, St Marylebone Church, two witnesses. On the envelope Robert writes as before: "Saturday, Septr. 12, 1846, ¼11—11¼ A.M. (91)." The wedding entered his count as their ninety-first meeting. After the church Elizabeth goes not with her husband but home. Next day the room is full of visitors, and suddenly bells ring. "'Marylebone Church bells' said Henrietta, standing behind my chair." A friend of the family drops in, and one of his first words is: "When did you see Browning?"

A week later she leaves the house with her maid and her spaniel. In his last letter the day before, Robert asks: "Write to me one word more." She writes: "Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?" She admits how dreadful it is "to have to give pain here by a voluntary act—for the first time in my life." And adds: "none are so bold as the timid, when they are fairly roused."

For a 9-6-6 couple this scene holds the whole mechanism of the middle. The Hermit says "not now" and waits sixteen months; the Lovers say "now or never", and the whole ending, the wedding and the departure, fits into a single week. In ordinary life the door is seldom locked by a father in Wimpole Street. More often it is closed by the two people's own caution: "let's not tell anyone yet", "let's talk about it later". Sometimes by a parent's voice that speaks in an argument before one's own. The middle is passed when the choice is spoken, at least to each other.

sections.h2: Sonnets handed over from behind: the main task
paragraphs: The two poets discussed their work in letters all the time, but Elizabeth did not show him her poems about him. On 22 July 1846 she writes: "You shall see some day at Pisa what I will not show you now. Does not Solomon say that 'there is a time to read what is written.' If he doesn't, he ought." Solomon said no such thing. Ecclesiastes has "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak". She rewrote the verse to suit herself.

What happened next was told by the critic Edmund Gosse in a book of 1896, from a statement Browning had made to a friend eight years before his death. The couple had a rule: to write alone and not show each other what they had written. Robert sometimes broke it; she never did. One morning after breakfast he stood at the window and became aware of someone behind him. It was Elizabeth. She **held him by the shoulder to prevent his turning to look at her**, and pushed a packet of papers into the pocket of his coat. She told him to read it and to tear it up if he did not like it, and fled to her room upstairs. The papers were sonnets about the two of them; the book has forty-four. He read them, ran upstairs and, in Gosse's words, "stormed that guarded citadel". Later he would say: "I dared not reserve to myself the finest sonnets written in any language since Shakespeare's."

This scene should be read as a family legend, not a record. Gosse placed it in Pisa in 1847 and cited a slim first edition, "Reading, 1847". In 1934 the bibliographers John Carter and Graham Pollard proved that edition a forgery by Thomas Wise, and biographers now date the day of the sonnets later. The only document is the July letter: "what I will not show you now".

When the sonnets were to be printed, they needed a title. Elizabeth proposed "Sonnets translated from the Bosnian". Robert replied: "No, not Bosnian—that means nothing—but from the Portuguese! They are Catarina's sonnets!" He had long called her his "own little Portuguese", and she had written a poem, "Catarina to Camoens", about a love just like this. Gosse calls the title **an ingenious device to veil the true authorship**. One of the most open books of English love poetry came out in 1850 in the mask of a translation.

The couple's main task is point D, and it is read mostly through the minus: what does not work and what there is to learn. The scene at the window shows it in one gesture. Elizabeth hands over the most open text of her life — that is the Lovers. But she does not let him see her face — that is the Hermit. The task of 9-6-6 is to turn around.
What stops people turning around is written in the same sonnets.

ul: **"Hard to love".** Sonnet XXXV: "Alas, I have grieved so I am hard to love. / Yet love me—wilt thou? Open thy heart wide". The Lovers in the task teach self-love inside the couple, and sometimes the other partner is the teacher.

**The fear of being loved as someone imagined.** As early as May 1845 she writes to Robert of his "mistakes in me", which "have humbled me by too much honouring". Sonnet XIV asks: "If thou must love me, let it be for nought / Except for love's sake only. Do not say / 'I love her for her smile—her look—her way / Of speaking gently'". These things "may be changed", and love so wrought "may be unwrought so". An ideal image of the partner is a burden here, not a gift.
**The need to hear it again.** Insecurity that is given no words looks for proof and easily turns into jealousy and control. Sonnet XXI turns it into a request said out loud.

paragraphs: Sonnet XXI begins: "Say over again, and yet once over again, / That thou dost love me." And it ends: "Say thou dost love me, love me, love me—toll / The silver iterance!—only minding, Dear, / To love me also in silence with thy soul."

These lines hold the answer to why the six repeats in this tail. The repeat does not mean twice as much love. It is one word in two roles. In the middle it is said for the first time, and what matters is not to burn it. In the main task it has to be said again and once over again, and silence is not driven out but invited in: "also in silence". In this tail the Hermit is not the enemy of the Lovers. He asks for a place beside them.

In 1855 Browning publishes the collection Men and Women, fifty poems in which, as usual, he speaks in other people's voices: a painter-monk, a knight, a painter. The last poem is called "One Word More" and is dedicated "To E. B. B.". It is what he asked of her in his last letter before the flight: "Write to me one word more." The echo is our observation, but it speaks for itself.
Only here does Browning speak without a mask: "Let me speak this once in my true person, / Not as Lippo, Roland or Andrea". And then come the lines that hold the whole 9-6-6 tail:
"God be thanked, the meanest of his creatures / Boasts **two soul-sides, one to face the world with, / One to show a woman when he loves her!**"

He calls her "my moon of poets". The moon, if she loved a mortal, would turn to him a side no one had seen, not Homer, not Galileo. The world sees her poems and praises them; he praises them along with everyone. "But the best is when I glide from out them… / Come out on the other side… / Where I hush and bless myself with silence."

The second mask shows here too. She hid her love behind a "translation from the Portuguese"; he was used to hiding behind other people's voices. Both took off their masks only for each other. This is the strong version of the tail: **the Hermit faces the world, the Lovers face each other**. Trouble starts when the cloak is turned inward and the two hide from each other what they keep from strangers. The Moon in the couple's values, found in three such couples out of ten, sounds especially close to these lines: the far side, shown to one person. This is our reading, not a rule of the method.

sections.h2: Lamp and cloak: the Hermit and the Lovers in Waite
paragraphs: Waite's drawing is not the card on the site, but two of its details hold this tail together.

Waite changed the old Hermit with a single stroke and said so himself: "The variation from the conventional models in this card is only that the lamp is not enveloped partially in the mantle of its bearer." "It is a star which shines in the lantern", and Waite calls this "a card of attainment". Half a century before his book, Browning had used the same word about himself in "One Word More": "I stand on my attainment."

The Lovers, as Waite describes them, are a man and a woman "unveiled before each other". Not before the world, but before each other. The whole tail fits between the two cards: from a lamp under a cloak to two people without veils.

Waite's divinatory lists read like a commentary on the story. For the Hermit: "Prudence, circumspection", and reversed: "Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution." The title Sonnets from the Portuguese is a disguise in the most literal sense. For the Lovers: "Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome", and reversed: "marriage frustrated and contrarieties of all kinds."

Elizabeth has a sonnet that reads like this card. In Sonnet XXII two souls stand "Face to face, silent, drawing nigh and nigher, / Until the lengthening wings break into fire". The angels would press on them, aspiring "To drop some golden orb of perfect song / Into our deep, dear silence." She asks instead to stay on earth, where "the unfit / Contrarious moods of men recoil away / And isolate pure spirits", and to have "A place to stand and love in for a day". The silence in this sonnet is not a wall between two people; it is what they share.

sections.h2: How the 9-6-6 circle turns in a couple's life
paragraphs: The beginning is nearly always quiet. The two prefer an evening under a lamp to a party, talk late into the night and understand each other from half a phrase. One silently fixes the other's bicycle; the other leaves the hall light on when the first comes home late. A year passes before they share a flat, and friends learn about the wedding from a photo. From outside they are a calm, slightly closed couple, and they like it that way.

The first crack appears where it did for the Brownings. One says something important too early: "I'm frighteningly happy with you", or "let's live together". The other goes silent, and the next day jokes: "let's forget it, that was the night talking". The word is filed under misprints, and both pretend it was never said.

Then a rule takes hold that nobody announced: write alone and don't show. Hurts wait in a drawer until some "Pisa", proposals go unspoken, drafts stay hidden. From outside the couple is as calm as ever; inside there are two rooms on different floors. In Pisa it was exactly so for the Brownings: he worked downstairs, she upstairs.

Then comes the minus of the Lovers. Insecurity grows in silence. One asks "do you still love me?", the other answers "I'm here, aren't I?" — for the Hermit, the deed is the answer. The first wants more, starts looking for proof, and the second feels examined. From there it is not far to checking and jealousy. Or to the other extreme: one sees the partner as an ideal, and the partner dares not step out of that image and hides whatever does not fit it.
The price of the circle is years of love that exists but is not said. Two hermits under one roof, each with a lantern, each sure the other knows anyway.
The way out is built into the cards. The Hermit does not need to be driven away, and the Lovers do not need to be proved. The cloak needs to be turned outward.

ul: **Say in words what has already been done in deeds.** The Lovers ask for the word; the Hermit thinks the deed is enough. Sonnet XXI asks for both.
**Don't ask for what was said to be forgotten.** If a partner said too much too soon, "I need time" is more honest than "let's pretend this never happened".
**Show the draft.** Not only the finished decision, but the doubt, the fear, the unfinished thought. In this couple the most important things often lie in a drawer.
**Decide out loud, to each other.** The world can be told afterwards, as the Hermit likes. Each other — at once.
**Turn around.** Hand over important things face to face, not from behind, and hold the look that comes back.
**Keep room for shared silence.** Silence chosen by two holds a union together. Silence in which each one hides pulls it apart.

sections.h2: The strong version of the 9-6-6 tail
paragraphs: In its strong version this couple stays quiet to the world and open inside. Its silence is the "deep, dear silence" of the sonnet, not a wall. The Hermit's lantern shines first for the two and then for others: such a couple can give sound advice, because it knows how to listen.

In the preface to the correspondence, the Brownings' son explained why there are exactly 573 letters and will be no more: they are "all that ever passed between my father and mother, for after their marriage they were never separated". The Hermit's language, the letter, ends where life face to face begins. Elizabeth's last letter asks: "Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?" The tail 9-6-6 puts the same question to the couple: when will the two stop talking through a box of letters and start speaking to each other face to face?

intro: The riddle is in the numbers themselves. A card of solitude opens the road, and then one and the same card stands twice, halfway along and at the end. No single person has this tail: in a personal matrix the middle is the sum of the two outer numbers, and between the Hermit and the Lovers it would hold the Devil (9 + 6 = 15). In a couple the middle is brought by two people, and it turns out to be love again.

ul: **M — "Entry to the task", 9, the Hermit.** What the two want together: quiet, depth, a conversation where half a word is enough. The couple enters its task through this wish, and the same wish is where it gets stuck.
**N — "Middle of the task", 6, the Lovers.** How the couple travels the road: through a word of love said out loud, and through a choice that cannot be made halfway.
**D — "Main task", 6, the Lovers.** What there is to learn: to love openly, to let yourself be seen and to believe you were chosen.

intro: The plot shows best in the story of two English poets, Elizabeth Barrett and Robert Browning. For twenty months they wrote each other letters, they married in secret, and she passed off her most open poems as a translation from the Portuguese. Nobody here calculates their matrix: the story is not proof but a mirror that shows how these three cards work.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-6-6 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail where the entry to the task is the Hermit (9), and the middle and the main task are the Lovers (6). The couple comes together through depth, quiet and a common language, travels the road through a word of love said aloud and a choice, and its main task is to love openly and let itself be seen, without hiding from each other what it hides from the world.

faq.q: Why is there no 9-6-6 tail in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of the entry and the main task: 9 + 6 would give 15, the Devil. In a couple's matrix every point is the sum of the same points of two people, and the middle is added up from the partners' middles, most often 7 + 17, 3 + 3 or 4 + 20. So 9-6-6 appears only in a couple.

faq.q: The Lovers appear twice — does that mean twice as much love?
faq.a: No. A repeated card does not double a quality; each six has its own role. In the middle the Lovers describe how the couple travels the road: through the first word of love and a choice. In the main task they describe what to learn: to repeat that word, to believe you were chosen, and not to hide what is imperfect from the partner.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers?
faq.a: No. The site's engine produces no other couple tail from a nine and two sixes, so 9-6-6 cannot be confused with a permutation: the order "entry — middle — main task" is the only one here.

faq.q: Is the tail 9-6-6 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events or pass verdicts; it describes a task. For these couples the Hermit is both the entry and, in seven couples out of ten, the value of the union. The difficulty is not the quiet itself, but the moment the quiet starts being kept from each other.

It occurs in roughly one couple in 97 (1.026%) and ranks 36th of the 97 couple tails. It is formed by nine combinations of the partners' personal tails; the most common are 3-7-22 + 6-17-11, 18-3-12 + 9-3-21 and 21-4-10 + 6-20-14.
